Tufted duck (Aythya fuligula) is a widespread diving duck that breeds across northern Eurasia, and its life history traits have been documented through field studies of wild populations and captive rearing programs. Newly hatched ducklings emerge weighing approximately 37.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 37.5 grams], a modest initial mass typical of precocial waterfowl that rapidly gain independence. Under artificial incubation conditions maintained at 36.65 °C [T = 36.65 °C], eggs complete their development and hatch after an average period of 26.5 days [ab = 26.5 days], a duration consistent with the incubation requirements reported for other Aythya species. The incubation temperature of 36.65 °C, derived from comparative analyses across waterfowl, appears critical for normal embryonic development. Upon hatching, the downy chicks are led to water almost immediately by the female, where they begin feeding on aquatic invertebrates. This precocial developmental strategy is reflected in the relatively low neonatal mass relative to the ultimate adult body size that the birds eventually attain, a pattern common among rapidly growing temperate waterfowl inhabiting productive wetland environments.

As the ducklings progress through their early development, they undergo a period of rapid somatic growth that culminates in the achievement of flight. Fledging occurs at approximately 52.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 52.5 days after hatching], with individual variation typically falling within the reported range of 49 to 56 days. This developmental milestone marks the transition to nutritional independence, after which the young birds begin to disperse from their natal wetlands. The fledging period is followed by a prolonged juvenile phase during which the immature birds continue to refine their foraging skills and accumulate body reserves. During this post-fledging interval, body mass increases substantially from the hatchling weight toward the dimensions characteristic of sexually mature adults. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown Tufted ducks from the species' core range has been recorded at 701.5 grams [Wwi = 701.5 grams], a value that reflects the moderate body size typical of this diving duck relative to other members of the genus Aythya that exploit similar benthic invertebrate prey resources.

The onset of sexual maturity in Tufted duck marks a significant transition in the individual's life cycle, occurring well after the completion of structural growth. Puberty is attained at 157.5 days after hatching [tp = 157.5 days after hatching], a timing that allows young birds to undergo a full cycle of feather molt and body condition recovery before their first potential breeding season. However, despite reaching gonadal maturity at this relatively early age, most individuals do not immediately engage in reproductive activity. Instead, the first successful breeding attempt is typically deferred until the following spring, when the birds are approximately one year old. The time since birth at first brood has been documented at 365 days [tR = 365 days], a pattern that aligns with the seasonal breeding constraints experienced by temperate-nesting waterfowl, where the availability of suitable nesting habitat and food resources is strongly pulsed by seasonal productivity cycles in boreal and subarctic wetlands.

Reproductive effort in female Tufted ducks is characterized by a moderate clutch size and a restricted annual breeding window. Field surveys consistently report that females lay between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch, with the majority of nests containing 8 to 10 eggs [N_R_i = nests containing 8 to 10 eggs], and they produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], reflecting the maximum reproductive output typical of this species in productive temperate wetlands. The maximum daily reproduction rate, derived from this combination, corresponds to approximately 9 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 9 offspring per year]. The relatively small clutch size compared to some sympatric dabbling ducks may reflect the higher energetic demands of diving for food during the laying and incubation period, as well as the need to balance reproductive investment against self-maintenance in a species that experiences significant wing molt costs. The incubation period itself, carried out exclusively by the female, lasts approximately 26 days, during which the incubating bird may lose up to 20% of her body mass due to the combined metabolic costs of egg warming and reduced foraging time. This concentrated reproductive strategy appears well suited to the short, productive summers characteristic of the species' boreal breeding grounds.

Longevity records for the Tufted duck indicate that this species possesses a moderately extended lifespan relative to its body size among diving ducks. The maximum recorded lifespan in wild populations reaches up to approximately 45.2 years [am = approximately 45.2 years], although such extreme ages are exceptional and most individuals likely survive for considerably shorter durations due to the cumulative risks of predation, disease, and harsh winter conditions encountered during migration. This considerable potential longevity is reflected in the species' life history strategy, which combines moderate annual reproductive output with the capacity for repeated breeding attempts across many seasons. Comparative analyses of survival and mortality suggest that adult survival rates are relatively high once birds reach breeding age, contributing to stable population dynamics across the species' range. The interplay between reproductive investment, fledging success, and adult survival continues to be a focus of demographic research, particularly as changing wetland conditions alter the availability of critical invertebrate prey resources across both breeding and wintering areas.
